title: Arthur After Hours

jokes.text: General rule of thumb... if you see nose hair, it's too close.
jokes.setup: Director is told not to zoom too close on Larry during the show.
jokes.punchline: Artie frames the camera distance rule in terms of visible nose hair — specific, visual, and deflating to Larry.
jokes.explanation: Crisp, specific, and perfectly economical. The nose-hair image is unexpectedly precise and funny, and it also sets up Larry's vanity/insecurity as a character motif. Artie's flat delivery implied here makes it work.

dialogue.line: General rule of thumb... if you see nose hair, it's too close. Aha!

jokes.text: Checks for Larry, birds for Hank... aw, throw that one away.
jokes.setup: Artie is going through production notes/instructions.
jokes.punchline: He appears to be sorting compliments for the hosts — then immediately dismisses the Hank version as not worth keeping.
jokes.explanation: A quick, casual dismissal of Hank that reveals the show's power hierarchy efficiently. The self-correction ('throw that one away') is the punchline delivered in the same breath, very natural and Artie-specific.

dialogue.line: Checks for Larry, birds for Hank... aw, throw that one away.

jokes.text: Gracias, hombre. Vamanos.
jokes.setup: Artie is giving instructions to a staff member, presumably not Latino.
jokes.punchline: He casually throws in Spanish dismissal as if it's standard operating procedure — an affectation that reveals his performative command persona.
jokes.explanation: A mild character quirk laugh — Artie's macho flourish. Not particularly original but consistent with his old-school showbiz bluster character. Mild chuckle at best.

dialogue.line: As much as I'd love Larry to ask her about her gorgeous new tits, I feel we covered that front quite well when miss butler was here in may.

jokes.text: As much as I'd love Larry to ask her about her gorgeous new tits, I feel we covered that front quite well when Miss Butler was here in May.
jokes.setup: Artie is reviewing interview questions for Brett Butler's upcoming segment.
jokes.punchline: He frames a deeply inappropriate topic ('gorgeous new tits') with the dry language of a TV producer checking off agenda items, as if it's a covered story beat.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Artie deploys the language of professional editorial judgment ('covered that front quite well') to justify the most crass possible content consideration. The collision of register is sharp. Very Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: You have to forgive me. I've got my period.

jokes.text: You have to forgive me. I've got my period. / Really? Yeah. / You know, you used that excuse 10 weeks ago, memory serves. That means you're not due to start your cycle until the 22nd or 23rd.
jokes.setup: Paula says she's spacey and excuses herself by claiming she has her period.
jokes.punchline: Artie, with alarming precision and zero self-awareness, cites the exact date of her last claim and calculates when her next cycle is due.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first major joke and one of its best. The layered absurdity — that Artie tracks this at all, that he has it memorized, that he delivers it with the matter-of-fact certainty of a stage manager — is perfectly calibrated cringe. It reveals his total lack of appropriate workplace boundaries while still feeling like a coherent character choice. The escalation ('you were a bit puffy') as confirmation makes it even better. Comparable in craft to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You know, you used that excuse 10 weeks ago, memory serves. That means you're not due to start your cycle until the 22nd or 23rd.

jokes.text: Well, how do you know I wasn't lying the last time? / You were a bit puffy.
jokes.setup: Paula tries to escape Artie's menstrual cycle tracking by suggesting she lied last time.
jokes.punchline: Artie confirms he monitored physical symptoms and offers 'puffy' as empirical evidence.
jokes.explanation: The two-word punchline 'You were a bit puffy' is the comedic zenith of this exchange. The economy is near-perfect — maximum implication (he watched her body) with minimum words. Paula's horrified pause before his follow-up about not being the first woman to tell him that makes this land as a full comedic sequence. The rewatch bonus applies because each line escalates the horror of what Artie has revealed.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Well, how do you know I wasn't lying the last time?

jokes.text: You're not the first woman who's told me that.
jokes.setup: Paula says 'you're good' in response to Artie correctly deducing her cycle from 'puffiness.'
jokes.punchline: Artie takes 'you're good' as a general compliment about himself, implying women regularly tell him this — missing the horror entirely.
jokes.explanation: The button on the sequence. Artie's oblivious self-satisfaction, reframing Paula's stunned acknowledgment as general female praise, is perfectly in character. The ambiguity of whether he's bragging about this specifically or in general is the joke's texture.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You were a bit puffy.

jokes.text: Do you like history, Phil? / What does that mean? / Because if Larry doesn't want to wear the hat, that's what it becomes, dig?
jokes.setup: Phil complains that Larry won't wear the hat for the Gorton's Fisherman sketch.
jokes.punchline: Artie opens with a seemingly non-sequitur about history, then reveals it means 'this will become history' — i.e., the sketch is dead, and Larry's will is final.
jokes.explanation: A clever bit of Artie-ism — the Socratic setup ('do you like history?') followed by the ruthlessly pragmatic punch about Larry's total authority. It's a sharp industry-insider joke about the power of the host. The 'dig?' caps it with period-specific cool.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, you're good. You're not the first woman who's told me that.

jokes.text: What makes you laugh, the sketch? / No. The word 'slicker' makes me chuckle. Say it again. / Slicker. / Use it in a sentence. / I like my slicker.
jokes.setup: Phil is furious about the sketch dying. Artie starts laughing.
jokes.punchline: Artie is not laughing at the sketch problem — he's just tickled by the word 'slicker' and makes Phil say it repeatedly, completely derailing the urgent conversation.
jokes.explanation: This is pure character comedy executed with precision. Artie's ability to be delighted by something completely inconsequential ('slicker') while a colleague is having a genuine crisis is a brilliant encapsulation of his zen-like refusal to be stressed. 'Use it in a sentence / I like my slicker' is a miniature absurdist routine dropped into a workplace drama. Genuinely exceptional for its category.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Do you like history, Phil? What does that mean? Because if Larry doesn't want to wear the hat, that's what it becomes, dig?

jokes.text: Artie, I'm gonna kick somebody's ass, I swear.
jokes.setup: Phil watches Artie giggle helplessly at the word 'slicker' while their sketch crisis is unresolved.
jokes.punchline: Phil's exasperated threat is the straight-man button on the sequence — his anger is funny precisely because Artie doesn't register it.
jokes.explanation: The straight-man button on the 'slicker' bit. Functional as a scene-closer but not funny on its own — it's the context that makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: He is supposed to be the gorton's fisherman. Without the hat, he's just a guy in a yellow slicker.

jokes.text: that wendy bitch in charge of the audience... she's got her way in the hell up there where we put the retards.
jokes.setup: Beverly is furious that her mother has been seated badly at the show taping.
jokes.punchline: Her complaint escalates to revealing where the 'bad seats' are by describing them with a deeply offensive term, delivered with complete conviction.
jokes.explanation: The joke is Beverly's complete lack of filter — the offensive term is delivered without malice, which is what makes it a character joke rather than shock comedy. Period-specific and uncomfortable by today's standards, but in context it's revealing Beverly's blunt working-class candor.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: What? Makes me laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: What makes you laugh, the sketch?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No. The word 'slicker' makes me chuckle.

jokes.text: We call them 'mentally challenged' now, Beverly.
jokes.setup: Beverly uses an offensive term for people with disabilities.
jokes.punchline: Artie's prim correction is delivered without breaking stride — he doesn't care, he's just noting the update.
jokes.explanation: Artie's total disengagement from Beverly's genuine distress, pivoting to an etiquette correction before immediately moving on, is funny for its tone-deafness. Economy is high — five words do the work.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Say it again. Slicker. Use it in a sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I like my slicker.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Ha ha.

jokes.text: Don't twist your skivvies in a knot, sugar. We'll put her right down front, OK?
jokes.setup: Beverly is escalating her fury about her mother's seating.
jokes.punchline: Artie deflates the crisis with an old-fashioned dismissive endearment ('don't twist your skivvies') and immediately solves the problem, making her rage feel disproportionate.
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'skivvies' phrasing and the breezy resolution is a mild character chuckle — his old-school paternal management style in miniature. 'Sugar' as an address to a furious woman is nicely condescending-oblivious.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Artie, I'm gonna kick somebody's ass, I swear.

jokes.text: Having fun showing her around? / Artie, the woman is my mother.
jokes.setup: Artie asks Beverly if she's enjoying showing her mother the show.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's 'she's my mother' is a deflating non-answer that implies the question was absurd — of course it's not 'fun,' it's an obligation.
jokes.explanation: A quick observational laugh about the mother-daughter dynamic — loving obligation is not 'fun.' Punchy and relatable but not elevated.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Profanity, beverly. I love it.

jokes.text: Is there blood? Everywhere.
jokes.setup: A staff member says Hank wants Artie urgently — it's an emergency.
jokes.punchline: Artie asks 'Is there blood?' to triage the severity. The response 'everywhere' — delivered deadpan — implies the emergency is still not worth his immediate attention.
jokes.explanation: Exquisite economy. Two words — 'Is there blood?' — establishes Artie's entire worldview about Hank's crises. The response 'everywhere' played completely straight suggests the respondent has learned to play along. The exchange burns only four words and lands hard. One of the episode's best micro-exchanges.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: that wendy bitch in charge of the audience... she's got her way in the hell up there where we put the retards.

jokes.text: What, can't find your way upstream to spawn?
jokes.setup: Artie finds Hank not yet in costume ten minutes before warm-up.
jokes.punchline: Artie's insult implies Hank should instinctively know to go get ready, like a salmon going upstream — the metaphor is absurd and slightly demeaning.
jokes.explanation: A nicely strange metaphor — comparing Hank to a salmon homing instinct is specific and slightly surreal. Artie's animal metaphors for Hank are a character signature.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: We call them 'mentally challenged' now, beverly.

jokes.text: This is about respect. This is about personal space. / Hey, skip to the end.
jokes.setup: Hank begins a serious declaration about respect and personal space regarding his karaoke machine.
jokes.punchline: Artie cuts him off with 'skip to the end' — treating Hank's manufactured gravitas as pure padding.
jokes.explanation: 'Skip to the end' is a lean, sharp dismissal that works universally but lands perfectly in the Artie/Hank dynamic. Hank's pomposity deflated in three words.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Don't twist your skivvies in a knot, sugar.

jokes.text: someone has been coming in here and just using this baby without my permission. I walk in the morning, the red light is on, and this baby is just warm to the touch, and I gotta tell ya, it's unsettling.
jokes.setup: Hank explains his karaoke machine crisis with mounting personal distress.
jokes.punchline: The escalating intimacy with which he describes the machine ('warm to the touch,' 'unsettling') is wildly disproportionate to the actual problem — it reads like he's describing a violated intimate object.
jokes.explanation: Hank's wounded dignity about something trivial is a core character comedy engine. 'Warm to the touch' is the specific detail that elevates this from generic complaint to genuine character revelation — his possessiveness and sense of violation over a karaoke machine is deeply, specifically Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Having fun showing her around?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Artie, the woman is my mother.

jokes.text: And not to get off the subject, but I think we could use this on the show and just have a lot of fun with it. / I think we could. / Really? / No.
jokes.setup: Hank pivots mid-complaint to pitch using his karaoke machine on the show, and Artie seems to agree.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Really? No.' — the false agreement followed by instant deflation — is a surgical rejection.
jokes.explanation: Perfect beat comedy. 'Really? No.' is a four-syllable punchline that encapsulates the entire producer-talent power dynamic. Artie lets Hank have a moment of hope and then removes it in the same breath. Structurally clean.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Is there blood? Everywhere.

jokes.text: I know how your people enjoy the karaoke. / It wasn't me, Hank. / Now if you'll excuse me, I must go call my parents and tell them I'm Asian.
jokes.setup: Hank suspects the staff of using his machine and tells Brian that Asian people enjoy karaoke, implying Brian is the culprit.
jokes.punchline: Brian responds to the racial stereotype with withering irony — going to call his parents to inform them of his ethnicity, as if Hank has revealed something Brian didn't know about himself.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The structure is impeccable: Hank's casual racism is played as oblivious Hank-ness (not evil), and Brian's response is a perfectly calibrated, completely deadpan skewering that exposes the absurdity without belaboring it. 'I must go call my parents and tell them I'm Asian' is highly quotable, earned by genuine wit rather than shock, and perfectly characterizes both men. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in craft and slightly above in quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: What, can't find your way upstream to spawn?

jokes.text: I miss Darlene. And not just because of, you know, the, uh, the sweaters.
jokes.setup: A male staff member mentions missing a colleague named Darlene.
jokes.punchline: He specifies 'not just because of the sweaters' — implying Darlene's sweaters (i.e., her figure in sweaters) was a primary reason, which he then catches himself on.
jokes.explanation: A small, well-placed aside. The self-correction ('not just because of') is the joke — he's admitting the sweaters were definitely part of it. Economical and lands as a passing laugh without overstaying.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: someone has been touching my karaoke machine.

jokes.text: You know, that was the least graceful entrance we've ever had on the show. / Would you expect anything less from moi?
jokes.setup: Sandra makes a chaotic entrance onto the set.
jokes.punchline: Larry calls it the least graceful entrance; Sandra owns it completely, recasting her lack of grace as a brand promise.
jokes.explanation: Sandra playing herself-as-character with self-aware abandon. 'Would you expect anything less from moi?' is confident and funny. The French 'moi' is an affectation that fits the Sandra persona. Good but not remarkable.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, God, no!

jokes.text: I would rather sometimes be allowed to be the man. / Well, you're gonna have a little bit of a fight on your hands.
jokes.setup: Larry and Sandra both walked in at the same time; Larry suggests he should have led.
jokes.punchline: Sandra's response implies she's not ceding the masculine energy role to Larry — a comment about both gender dynamics and the power balance between them.
jokes.explanation: Sharp in the context of Sandra's persona and Larry's insecurity. It lightly undermines Larry's masculinity while being characterful for Sandra. Functional, professional-grade.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Heh heh. Look at you in a shawl-collar jacket.
jokes.setup: Sandra looks at Larry's outfit.
jokes.punchline: The laugh before the comment — and the specificity of 'shawl-collar jacket' — implies it's a mild fashion crime that amuses her.
jokes.explanation: Visual gag inferred from dialogue — Sandra's amused reaction to Larry's specific jacket. Mild fashion-ribbing, works in the moment but doesn't read especially well in transcript form.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I walk in the morning, the red light is on, and this baby is just warm to the touch

jokes.text: It is... no, it's a fashion do-do-do-do... ♪ do-do-do-do-do-do-do ♪ / Wow. Gee whiz. I wish I could do that.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if his jacket is a fashion 'don't'; Sandra begins to answer and then breaks into the Addams Family-style do-do-do-do riff.
jokes.punchline: Sandra derails the conversation with an improvisational musical non-answer; Larry's 'gee whiz, I wish I could do that' is a brilliantly deadpan response to her unpredictability.
jokes.explanation: Larry's 'gee whiz' deadpan is the real laugh here — his resigned bewilderment at Sandra's energy is perfectly Larry. This is the show at its talk-show satire best: the host slightly outgunned by the guest.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I know how your people enjoy the karaoke.

jokes.text: You're bitter about the Lisa Marie-Michael Jackson thing, aren't you? I picture you bitter. You wanted to be with one of them.
jokes.setup: They're discussing the Lisa Marie-Michael Jackson relationship.
jokes.punchline: Sandra projects onto Larry that he wanted to be romantically involved with one of them — a casually weird insinuation delivered as settled fact.
jokes.explanation: Sandra Bernhard as a character is the agent of deliberate discomfort here — she psychoanalyzes Larry on air, which is exactly what the real Larry Sanders would hate. 'I picture you bitter' is a nice specific detail.

dialogue.speaker: Bri
dialogue.line: Now if you'll excuse me, I must go call my parents and tell them I'm asian.

jokes.text: I went over to Lisa Marie and Michael Jackson's house. I got into bed with them. They had plenty of room. I don't know what the problem is.
jokes.setup: Discussion of the Michael Jackson-Lisa Marie Presley marriage.
jokes.punchline: Sandra casually inserts herself into their bed as a known fact, then notes 'plenty of room' — implying a non-consummated marriage via the spatial metaphor.
jokes.explanation: The joke operates on multiple levels: it's a celebrity insult, it's a comment on the celebrity-marriage-as-spectacle, and 'plenty of room' is a slyly economical way to say what she's really implying about the relationship. Sandra-specific in its brazen delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I miss darlene. And not just because of, you know, the, uh, the sweaters.

jokes.text: They're arguing, or they're burying stuff in the backyard?
jokes.setup: Sandra says Jackson and Presley are 'going at it like cats and dogs.'
jokes.punchline: Larry asks if that means fighting or 'burying stuff in the backyard' — a darkly specific reference to animal behavior (cats bury things) that's also a veiled innuendo about secrets.
jokes.explanation: Larry's follow-up extends the 'cats and dogs' metaphor literally, which is an absurdist riff. The 'burying stuff in the backyard' implication (secrets? bodies?) adds a dark layer. Good comedic instinct from Larry-as-interviewer.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You know, that was the least graceful entrance we've ever had on the show.

jokes.text: for all I know... they're going out.
jokes.setup: Sandra has been building up analysis of the Jackson-Presley relationship with innuendo.
jokes.punchline: After all the implications, she lands on the most banal possible conclusion — 'they're going out' — as if dating is the mildest revelation.
jokes.explanation: The anticlimax is the joke — 'for all I know, they're going out' after all the insinuation deflates expectation comedically. Classic misdirection/understatement button.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I would rather sometimes be allowed to be the man.

jokes.text: Everything's happening. All at once, they're just coming at me 100,000 miles a minute. / Who is? / Everybody in the business. / Is that a good thing that they're coming at you 100,000 miles... / Apparently, it's a nightmare.
jokes.setup: Sandra declares her career is going great with hyperbolic enthusiasm.
jokes.punchline: Larry (and the audience) can't get a handle on what's actually happening — the punchline is 'apparently, it's a nightmare,' reversing the setup completely.
jokes.explanation: The reversal is sharp and quick. 'Apparently, it's a nightmare' after breathless enthusiasm about success is a self-deprecating turn that plays against expectation. Good talk-show comedy rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: ♪ do-do-do-do-do-do-do ♪

jokes.text: I could stay here all fucking night. / Good. I adore you. Do anything for you.
jokes.setup: Larry asks Sandra to stay for another segment.
jokes.punchline: Sandra drops 'all fucking night' as if she's not on a broadcast (HBO), and Larry responds with identical warmth — their mutual performance of adoration is both genuine and slightly hollow.
jokes.explanation: The show-within-the-show meta-commentary — the in-character affection between Larry and Sandra feels like professional warmth. 'All fucking night' on HBO is an in-joke about the premium cable freedom. Mild.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: I got into bed with them. They had plenty of room.

jokes.text: I have an erection. / Funny, so do I. / Hey, 2 erections and nowhere to go.
jokes.setup: During the commercial break, Larry and Sandra are talking backstage.
jokes.punchline: Larry's erection comment is a (presumably joking) expression of excitement; Sandra matches it, and they turn it into a mutual complaint — '2 erections and nowhere to go.'
jokes.explanation: The joke works because of Sandra's persona — her claiming an erection is consistent with her gender-bending energy, and the duo turning it into mutual frustration ('nowhere to go') is a quick comedic escalation. The 'ouch' response suggests physical comedy or reaction beat follows.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: They're arguing, or they're burying stuff in the backyard?

jokes.text: You know, it's called Faithful, which I would like to be.
jokes.setup: Artie mentions Ryan O'Neal's new film with Cher, called 'Faithful.'
jokes.punchline: He appends 'which I would like to be' — a throwaway personal admission that implies he has infidelity issues, delivered so casually it barely registers as self-revelation.
jokes.explanation: A perfect aside — so economically delivered it's almost throwaway, but the character depth it implies (Artie, the old bachelor, wishing he could be faithful) rewards attention. The rewatch bonus is for catching the pathos.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: All at once, they're just coming at me 100,000 miles a minute. Who is? Everybody in the business.

jokes.text: Is this about me? / No, this isn't about you.
jokes.setup: Artie says 'I would like to be faithful' and Larry immediately asks if it's about him.
jokes.punchline: Larry's reflexive narcissism — assuming Artie's personal aside is actually a comment on Larry — is the joke. Artie's weary 'No, this isn't about you' confirms the pattern.
jokes.explanation: A tight two-line exchange that says everything about Larry's narcissism. 'Is this about me?' is the show's thesis in four words. The character integration is extremely high — no other character in the episode would ask this.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Not a damn thing. I've been fired off everything.
No, you haven't.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: I'm kidding.

jokes.text: Tell Farrah and Tatum and the others I said hi.
jokes.setup: Ryan O'Neal is being sent away after being bumped; Artie is doing a warm send-off.
jokes.punchline: 'The others' — after naming two of O'Neal's famous former lovers by first name, Artie bundles in an unspecified harem of others, acknowledging O'Neal's well-documented romantic history with a conspiratorial wink.
jokes.explanation: 'And the others' is the punchline — its vagueness is funnier than any specificity would be. It implies knowledge of a long list without cataloguing it, and it lets Ryan absorb it without protest. Very Artie — the kind of remark that can't quite be called an insult.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I have an erection.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Funny, so do I.

jokes.text: I rented Barry Lyndon the other night, you haven't aged a day, you dog.
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to smooth things over with Ryan O'Neal after bumping him from the show.
jokes.punchline: Artie compliments Ryan by referencing a 1975 film — the compliment is accidentally a reminder that it's been 20 years since Ryan was in his prime.
jokes.explanation: The joke is the gap between Artie's intention (compliment) and the actual effect (age reminder). 'You haven't aged a day' after citing a 20-year-old film is an unintentional insult about aging — and Ryan clearly doesn't take it well. Artie's obliviousness here mirrors his calendar tracking of Paula's cycle.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Hey, 2 erections and nowhere to go.

jokes.text: And the next time you need somebody to pick you up after one of your DUIs, don't call me.
jokes.setup: Ryan O'Neal is furious at Artie for being bumped and is escalating the confrontation.
jokes.punchline: Ryan reveals he's been picking Artie up from DUIs — a piece of very specific, very embarrassing personal information used as a weapon in an argument, but also confirming the depth of their friendship.
jokes.explanation: The DUI revelation lands because it's simultaneously an attack and a proof of genuine friendship — you only know someone's DUI history if you're actually close. It also characterizes Artie with a dark biographical detail (multiple DUIs) that enriches the character without being played for pity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hey, thanks for being a soldier about this, rye bread.

jokes.text: Speaking of my ass, if it gets any bigger, it's gonna need a publicist. I'm not kidding. It's gonna have a career of its own soon.
jokes.setup: Larry tells Artie to stop covering for him when he sells out others — 'you wipe it all over me.'
jokes.punchline: Larry pivots from serious grievance to complaining about his growing ass, which will soon need a publicist and have its own career.
jokes.explanation: The non-sequitur mid-argument pivot to body anxiety is classic Larry Sanders — his narcissism intrudes even in moments of genuine conflict. 'It's gonna need a publicist' is the escalation that makes it funny, extending the metaphor with showbiz logic. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Make you feel better to hit me? Go ahead. Shut up. You know you want to.

dialogue.speaker: Ryan
dialogue.line: I'm not hitting anymore.

jokes.text: Of course, that's what you'd think because you're such a brilliant judge of what people are feeling. / Thank you.
jokes.setup: Larry sarcastically attacks Artie's emotional intelligence.
jokes.punchline: Artie takes the sarcasm completely at face value and thanks Larry sincerely — either he genuinely misses the sarcasm, or he's playing it so straight it doesn't matter.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. The joke is maximally economical — Larry's sarcasm is delivered perfectly, and Artie's 'Thank you' in response is either (a) oblivious or (b) Artie choosing to absorb the compliment rather than the attack. Either reading is character-perfect. The line will pay off immediately in the episode (joke #42). Comparable in craft to the 8.0 anchor — same economy, same character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Ryan
dialogue.line: And the next time you need somebody to pick you up after one of your d.u.I. S, don't call me.

jokes.text: She's probably screwing Hans Brinker. She's making his skates into earrings as we speak.
jokes.setup: Larry's ex-wife is calling from the Netherlands.
jokes.punchline: Larry speculates she's sleeping with the legendary Dutch figure skater Hans Brinker, and then extends the image to her making his skates into earrings — a surreally specific detail.
jokes.explanation: The 'making his skates into earrings' detail is genuinely funny — it extends the Netherlands joke into absurdist specific territory. Hans Brinker is an obscure enough reference to feel clever rather than lazy. Larry's bitter wit in personal situations is a key character note.

dialogue.speaker: Ryan
dialogue.line: And don't call me rye bread. It's what farrah calls me.

jokes.text: Oh, he's upset. / Oh, you think? / Yes, I think so. That's what I'm picking up. I've been told I'm a good judge of what people are feeling. / I'm guessing he's upset. / That's not my problem now, is it, sweetie?
jokes.setup: Larry has stormed off angry. Artie and Larry observe that the person is upset.
jokes.punchline: Artie pointedly says 'I've been told I'm a good judge of what people are feeling' — a direct callback to Larry's sarcasm — and delivers it with total self-possession, turning the earlier insult into a compliment he now owns.
jokes.explanation: The callback fully pays off joke #41. Artie has absorbed the sarcasm, converted it to sincere self-praise, and now wields it — 'I've been told I'm a good judge of what people are feeling' — while correctly reading an upset man leaving the room. It's a small structural masterpiece: the joke was planted, paid off, and then weaponized. 'That's not my problem now, is it, sweetie?' is the cherry — dismissive, warm, final.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Speaking of my ass, if it gets any bigger, it's gonna need a publicist. I'm not kidding. It's gonna have a career of its own soon.

jokes.explanation: Mild Larry character comedy — his performative toughness on the phone with his ex. 'Them's the rules, baby' is slightly funny as affected toughness but not sharp.

jokes.explanation: The escalating Netherlands geography bit is a little constructed setup for a punchline, but the rhythm works — Rotterdam/Amsterdam build to 'I Don't Give a Damn' as a natural next step on the map. 'Bye, now' seals it with cheerful cruelty. High quotability because of the geography logic.

jokes.explanation: Larry's narcissistic self-appreciation of his own joke is a character beat that enriches the previous joke. 'OK, Larry' is a beautiful two-syllable Artie response — he's seen a thousand of these.

jokes.setup: Larry returns expecting to find a person he was arguing with — who has obviously left.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Of course. You didn't really expect to find him here' implies this is an established pattern — people leave when Larry makes himself available.
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat — Artie as the wry observer of Larry's interpersonal patterns. Functional but not elevated.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: go to rotterdam, then you go to amsterdam, then you go down the road to my city. That's right. It's a little place called I don't give a damn.

jokes.setup: Larry is alone on the empty stage after the argument, venting about the absent person.
jokes.punchline: His profanity escalates to include himself ('Fuck me') — he's so worked up he's turned on himself, which is the most Larry Sanders thing possible.
jokes.explanation: 'Fuck me for taking this shit so long' is the self-aware turn — Larry recognizes his own pattern mid-rage. It's both funny and slightly pathetic, which is the Larry Sanders sweet spot.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Of course. You didn't really expect to find him here.

jokes.text: Beverly? / I'm coming, ma!
jokes.setup: Artie calls Beverly's name after Larry's outburst, presumably to check on Larry or give direction.
jokes.punchline: Beverly, distracted (presumably tending to her mother), responds 'I'm coming, ma!' — confusing Artie's voice for her mother's call, or momentarily breaking frame.
jokes.explanation: The quick cut to Beverly responding to an imagined call from her mother — while at her work post — is a neat character beat. The mother subplot pays off with a laugh here.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: He's lucky he's not in that chair, the fucking asshole. Fuck him! Fuck me for taking this shit for so long!

jokes.text: And now, because he's a big, phony bastard... Larry Sanders!
jokes.setup: Hank is introducing Larry Sanders with the standard build-up.
jokes.punchline: The standard introduction is interrupted by Hank's genuine (if low-voiced) contempt — 'because he's a big, phony bastard' — before pivoting to the public-facing announcement.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best moments. The structure is perfect: the audience expects 'And now, because he's... [superlative]... Larry Sanders!' and instead gets Hank's genuine disdain inserted in the gap. Hank saying what he really thinks at the precise moment professional obligation requires the opposite is a distillation of the show's entire premise. 'Big, phony bastard' is exactly what Hank would think and exactly what he'd never normally say aloud. Highly quotable, rewatch-rewarding.

jokes.setup: Artie encourages Hank before the show; Hank introduces Artie to someone nearby.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'What a kiss-ass' is directed at himself — he's self-aware enough to know his own encouraging production-side behavior reads as sycophancy.
jokes.explanation: Artie's self-deprecating aside is a quick, good laugh — the veteran producer who knows every move he makes is slightly performative calling himself out for it. Economy is high.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: There's those letters I hate. There they are. I hate those fucking letters.

jokes.setup: Artie has been singing alone on the empty stage late at night and finds someone watching from the shadows.
jokes.punchline: The aggressor (Artie) discovers a Romanian janitor who was moved by his singing — and the janitor's broken English ('I janitor. I hear that sing. Very good.') undercuts any menace.
jokes.explanation: The scene pivot is well-constructed — Artie's macho 'I'm talking to you, asshole!' collapses immediately upon encountering a humble janitor who just liked the song. The setup-to-reversal is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And now, because he's a big, phony bastard, Larry Sanders!

jokes.text: Where are you from? / Toluca Lake in California. / Yeah, I recognize that Toluca Lake accent. / No, dipshit. I mean recently, before Toluca Lake.
jokes.setup: Artie asks where Nicolae is from, expecting a foreign country.
jokes.punchline: Nicolae answers 'Toluca Lake in California' — technically correct but not what was meant. Artie's deadpan 'I recognize that Toluca Lake accent' before correcting himself with 'No, dipshit' is the comic escalation.
jokes.explanation: The Toluca Lake gag is a lovely two-beat: the false answer, then Artie's sarcastic acceptance of it ('I recognize that Toluca Lake accent'), then his self-correction ('No, dipshit'). The rhythm is crisp and the 'dipshit' aimed at himself is a nice Artie touch.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Yeah, I recognize that toluca lake accent.

jokes.text: You watch the show? / Yes. / You like it? / Yes. / You watch it a lot? / Yes. / Who Larry is?
jokes.setup: Artie is showing Nicolae the set and confirming he watches the show.
jokes.punchline: After repeatedly affirming he watches and enjoys the show, Nicolae asks 'Who Larry is?' — he has apparently never registered the host of the show he watches regularly.
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully constructed joke. The buildup of 'Yes/Yes/Yes' creates complete confidence that Nicolae is a devoted viewer — making 'Who Larry is?' a perfect comedic reversal. It works on multiple levels: it's funny as a punchline, it's a meta-comment on Larry's ego (the show's host is unrecognizable to his own audience), and the grammatical structure of 'Who Larry is?' is perfectly timed broken English. Strong economy, strong structure.

dialogue.speaker: Artie

jokes.text: Hank. Hank is very good. / Ha! You know Hank? / Hey now!

jokes.punchline: Nicolae knows Hank and can even do Hank's catchphrase 'Hey now!' — but had no idea who Larry Sanders is. The sidekick is more recognizable than the host.
jokes.explanation: The callback extends and perfects joke #54. Not only does Nicolae not know Larry, he enthusiastically knows Hank — the sidekick — and can even perform the catchphrase. This is a sustained character joke that rewards everything the show has built: Hank's ego, Larry's insecurity, and the absurdity of celebrity. 'Hey now!' from a Romanian janitor is a perfect punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You just told me that you watch the show a lot.

jokes.text: Oh, God, I wish Larry were here right now. / Hey now. / Hey now!
jokes.setup: The discovery that Nicolae knows Hank but not Larry.
jokes.punchline: Artie wishes Larry were there to witness this humiliation — his absence is what makes the joke hurt. Then they repeat 'Hey now!' enthusiastically, rubbing it in.
jokes.explanation: Artie's delight in Larry's absence-humiliation — 'I wish Larry were here right now' — is a perfect payoff for the Larry/Artie tension. The repeated 'Hey now' as celebration is the running gag escalation. Good.

dialogue.speaker: Nicolae
dialogue.line: Hank. Hank is very good. Ha! You know Hank? Hey now!

jokes.text: You know why we get along, nic? 'Cause we're brothers. We're the unsung heroes. I clean up shit all day, you clean up shit all night. It's different shit, but we're the guys pushing the broom.
jokes.setup: Artie is bonding with Nicolae over shared working-class identity.
jokes.punchline: Artie the Hollywood veteran producer characterizes his work as cleaning up shit, equating himself with a janitor — the reductionism is both sincere and funny.
jokes.explanation: This is the thematic heart of the episode delivered as comedy. Artie's self-identification with the janitor ('we're the guys pushing the broom') is funny because it's slightly grandiose and slightly true simultaneously. 'It's different shit' is the key line — the qualifier that makes it not just sentimental but observed.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You know why we get along, nic? 'Cause we're brothers. We're the unsung heroes. I clean up shit all day, you clean up shit all night.

jokes.text: See, glenlivet? Single malt. When you die, you'll go to heaven, you say hello to God, and when God says hello to you, this is what you'll smell on his breath.
jokes.setup: Artie pours scotch for Nicolae and wants to explain what it is.
jokes.punchline: Artie's description escalates to God's breath smelling of Glenlivet — presenting it as sacred knowledge rather than a whiskey recommendation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable lines. Artie's rhetorical escalation — from 'single malt' to 'this is what God's breath smells like' — is perfectly structured and completely in character. It's absurdist in its theological specificity, it's character-perfect for a man of Artie's vintage and reverence for quality, and it's economically delivered. Compares favorably to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: When you die, you'll go to heaven, you say hello to God, and when God says hello to you, this is what you'll smell on his breath.

jokes.text: I'm sick of looking at this fucking picture here. It's going, it's gone. Bye-bye.
jokes.setup: Artie is roaming the set late at night, drinking with Nicolae.
jokes.punchline: He impulsively removes a picture from the wall — a small act of drunk authority over the workspace. The 'bye-bye' is a cheerful diminutive for what is presumably a rash decision.
jokes.explanation: A small, funny character moment — Artie drunk-exercising his producer authority on a picture. 'Bye-bye' as the farewell to a piece of décor is mild but charming.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You're lucky, nic, 'cause the shit I clean up talks back.

jokes.text: You're lucky, nic, 'cause the shit I clean up talks back.
jokes.setup: Artie continues the 'we both clean up shit' metaphor about their shared janitor identity.
jokes.punchline: The distinguishing feature of Artie's 'shit' (talent, stars, executives) is that it 'talks back' — a neat escalation of the metaphor that also perfectly describes show business.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the 'cleaning up shit' metaphor delivers a perfect one-liner: 'the shit I clean up talks back.' This is close to the episode's best single line. It extends the metaphor cleanly, it's maximally economical, it's deeply character-specific (a producer describing stars), and it's highly quotable in a way that transfers beyond the episode. High craft.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'm gonna resist the urge to, uh, express my anger by using profanity, and I hope you appreciate that, you... scum-sucking asshole!

jokes.text: I'm going to resist the urge to express my anger by using profanity, and I hope you appreciate that, you... scum-sucking asshole!
jokes.setup: Artie leaves a voice message for Larry, pledging to take the high road and not use profanity.
jokes.punchline: He immediately violates his own pledge in the same breath — 'scum-sucking asshole' — and then continues as if nothing happened.
jokes.explanation: The structure here is nearly perfect. The pledge ('I'm going to resist... using profanity') is the setup; the immediate violation ('you... scum-sucking asshole!') is the punchline; and the resumption of calm ('I've given this a great deal of thought') is the button. It's a three-beat comedic structure delivered without pause. The escalation across the voicemail — each self-imposed civility pledge followed by a new insult — is one of the episode's extended comedic highlights. This is professional-grade construction.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I wish you great success with the show. And personally, I have no ill will toward you... but hope your balls fall off.

jokes.text: I think the best thing for me to do is to move on, you... limp-dicked pantywaist.
jokes.setup: Artie continues the voicemail, again pledging to take the high road.
jokes.punchline: 'Limp-dicked pantywaist' — the insult after the second pledge is more specific and inventive than the first, escalating both in absurdity and specificity.
jokes.explanation: The escalation in the voicemail series — each new pledge followed by a more creative insult — peaks here with 'limp-dicked pantywaist,' which is one of the best pure insults in the episode. The archaic compound construction ('pantywaist') is Artie-specific; a younger character wouldn't reach for this. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: but does it crack? Does it? No!

jokes.text: I want you to know that I wish you great success with the show. / And personally, I have no ill will toward you... but hope your balls fall off.
jokes.setup: Artie wraps up the voicemail with professional well-wishing.
jokes.punchline: 'But hope your balls fall off' — the ultimate violation of the civility frame, and the darkest of the three curses.
jokes.explanation: The third beat of the voicemail sequence and its finest. 'I have no ill will toward you... but hope your balls fall off' is a near-perfectly constructed ironic wish — the civility of 'no ill will' followed by the most specific anatomical curse. 'Hope your balls fall off' will become the episode's most-quoted line. The voicemail sequence as a three-part escalation is one of the show's best sustained comedy bits.

dialogue.speaker: Artie

jokes.punchline: Artie cheerfully returns to a normal goodbye tone ('OK, take care') after three escalating profane insults — the tonal whiplash is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The button on the voicemail bit. 'OK, take care' after 'hope your balls fall off' is the tonal reset that confirms Artie is emotionally fine — the whole voicemail was catharsis, not distress.

jokes.explanation: The economy of 'Good. Big.' as a complete endorsement of Romanian women is very funny — the broken English stripped to essentials lands as deadpan understatement. Two words doing maximum work.

dialogue.speaker: Artie

jokes.punchline: Nicolae's immediate question 'She big?' confirms his assessment criterion — and Artie's 'Oh, good' implies she meets the standard.
jokes.explanation: The callback on 'big' as Nicolae's sole criterion is quick and funny. Artie's showbiz instinct to matchmake even late at night on an empty set is consistent character work.

jokes.text: Hey, nic, take a look up there. See all those beams there? How they're all tied together? There's an architectural term for that. I don't know what the hell it is, but they should call it the Arthur. Is the Arthur. That's right. Because all the pressure in this building, all the stress goes right into that... but does it crack? Does it? / No! / Aw, say, you bet your ass. Damn right it doesn't.
jokes.setup: Artie, drunk and philosophical, points out the structural beams of the stage.
jokes.punchline: He proposes naming the architectural stress structure 'The Arthur' because he, like the beams, absorbs all the pressure. He doesn't know the actual term — he just knows they should rename it after him.
jokes.explanation: This is the thematic and comedic centerpiece of the episode. Artie's drunk architectural soliloquy — proposing to rename the structural support beams after himself — is both funny and moving. The comedy comes from the specificity ('I don't know what the hell it is, but they should call it the Arthur'), the grandiosity (naming a structural element after yourself), and the sincerity (he genuinely believes this). Character integration is near-perfect: this speech could only come from Artie, in this moment, to this audience. The 'Does it crack?' / 'No!' call-and-response with Nicolae is a delightful touch.

dialogue.line: he gave me this the year he took his show to Florida.

jokes.text: 'cause all people remember is the night the chimp grabbed Larry's balls.
jokes.setup: Artie has been philosophizing about the meaning of his work — night after night of effort.
jokes.punchline: The summation of a career's legacy: not the good shows, not the craft — just the night a chimpanzee grabbed the host's genitals.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke and among the series' best. The buildup is all philosophical weight — work, legacy, meaning — and then Artie lands on 'the night the chimp grabbed Larry's balls' as the definitive public memory of his professional life. It's dark (career reduced to genitalia), it's specific (a chimp, not a generic animal), it's industry-insider (TV is just spectacle), and it's deeply character-specific (Artie's weary dignity next to this absurd legacy). The specificity elevates it above generic self-pity comedy. Comparable to the highest-scoring anchors.

jokes.explanation: The callback is perfectly placed — Nicolae has internalized 'hope they fall off' as the correct response to any mention of balls, misapplying the curse from enemy (Larry) to victim (Larry's chimp-attacked balls). 'Oh, settle down. We're not doing that right now' is Artie managing his student's enthusiasm. Great economy and callback construction.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You're still the fucking janitor, aren't you?

jokes.setup: Artie is lamenting his show-business life and its reduced legacy.
jokes.punchline: He catches himself mid-pity, looks at Nicolae (a Romanian janitor in America), and recalibrates — 'Look at you, you poor bastard.' The perspective shift is both funny and generous.
jokes.explanation: Artie's self-aware course-correction — he was complaining to someone who has actual hardship — is both funny and humanizing. 'You poor bastard' is affectionate-insult that works. The 'bet your whole ass' idiom is Artie-specific language.

dialogue.speaker: Nicolae
dialogue.line: I hope your balls falling off!

jokes.text: Look, the great one... Mr. Jackie Gleason himself... God love ya, buddy... he gave me this the year he took his show to Florida. / I want you to have it. / No. / Yeah. / No, it's yours because you're my brother.
jokes.setup: Artie gives a Jackie Gleason-gifted watch to Nicolae as a gesture of brotherhood.
jokes.punchline: Nicolae's repeated refusals — and Artie's insistence — is a comedic dance of pride and generosity that's also slightly pathetic (giving away a precious memento while drunk).
jokes.explanation: The setup for what becomes the bottle-smashing sequence and the watch dispute. Funny in its Old Guys Being Sentimental register, but the real payoff comes later. The Gleason namedrop is Artie's world — vintage showbiz mythology — and it enriches the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Nicolae

jokes.text: Look, the great one... Mr. Jackie Gleason himself... God love ya, buddy... he gave me this the year he took his show to Florida. I want you to have it.
jokes.setup: Artie tries to give Nicolae money from a money clip.
jokes.punchline: The money clip was given to Artie by Jackie Gleason — a piece of comedy royalty — and he's handing it off to a Romanian janitor he met an hour ago. The 'God love ya, buddy' addressed to Gleason (now dead) is a small, tender joke within the moment.
jokes.explanation: The Gleason detail is both funny (a money clip from Jackie Gleason is ending up in a Romanian janitor's hands) and deeply character-revealing (Artie exists in a world where such objects circulate and are given away as tokens of brotherhood). The comedy comes from the incongruity of the transaction.

dialogue.speaker: Nicolae
dialogue.line: I union. Union this!

jokes.text: Oh, what the... oh, there goes Glen. / I'm sorry, brother. / Aw, that's... what the hell. Just get your mop and clean it up.
jokes.setup: In the sentimental moment, a bottle of Glenlivet is apparently knocked over/broken.
jokes.punchline: Artie mourns 'Glen' (the Glenlivet) as if it were a person — 'there goes Glen' — and then pragmatically tells the janitor to clean it up.
jokes.explanation: Personifying the Glenlivet as 'Glen' — a fallen comrade — pays off the earlier God's-breath speech beautifully. And the immediate pivot to 'just get your mop and clean it up' is Artie's pragmatic management persona reasserting itself. Good callback structure.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: He's smiling like that because his refund check from the Betty ford clinic just came in the mail today.

jokes.text: Is bullshit. / What? What bullshit? / Why Nicolae get mop? Brother, you throw bottle. You go clean. / Oh, ho ho. Well, excuse me, brother. / You're still the fucking janitor, aren't you?
jokes.setup: Artie tells the janitor Nicolae to clean up the broken Glenlivet.
jokes.punchline: Nicolae objects: Artie threw the bottle, so Artie should clean it up. Artie's response — 'you're still the fucking janitor, aren't you?' — immediately reverts to class hierarchy after all the 'brotherhood' talk.
jokes.explanation: This is a masterful subversion of the brotherhood theme. The entire 'we're brothers' / 'you're me up there in those beams' speech is punctured in one line: 'You're still the fucking janitor, aren't you?' The hypocrisy is devastating, funny, and completely human. It takes everything the episode has built about Artie's generosity and undercuts it with his class reflexes. High craft because the joke earns its punch through narrative investment.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Prick.

jokes.text: Go to hell. / Fuck you. / Go to hell. / Ah...
jokes.setup: Artie and Nicolae are now in a genuine argument over the bottle clean-up.
jokes.punchline: The argument devolves into the two men trading 'go to hell' and 'fuck you' — a surprisingly equal exchange given their power difference.
jokes.explanation: The rapid-fire exchange is a comedy rhythm beat — two men of wildly different status throwing identical obscenities at each other. Funny for its escalation and equality, but the specific words aren't elevated.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Everything is Dan-Dan-dandy.

jokes.text: Here. Here. Money's back, clip is back. Take. / I no want. / Ah, you're a fucking idiot, you know that?
jokes.setup: After the argument, Artie tries to return the money and clip he gave Nicolae.
jokes.punchline: Nicolae refuses the return gift — 'I no want' — and Artie's frustrated response ('you're a fucking idiot') to a man refusing free money is the inversion.
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of insulting someone for refusing money. 'I no want' is a perfect four-syllable non-acceptance that enrages Artie. The pride contest between two men is consistent with both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Warm, moist, muffin-y goodness. Courtney Cox? Oh, close. A muffin.

jokes.text: Gimme my watch. / Watch I keep. / Aw, get your ass back here. / I hope your balls falling off! / Ah, fuck you. You're fired. / I union. Union this!
jokes.setup: The fight escalates to the Jackie Gleason watch.
jokes.punchline: Nicolae deploys the 'hope your balls fall off' curse back at Artie; Artie fires him; Nicolae reveals he's union and gives the universal union gesture. The callback of the curse and the union protection are perfect.
jokes.explanation: A perfect escalation sequence with multiple callbacks firing simultaneously: the 'balls fall off' curse returns (now aimed at Artie), the class hierarchy is exposed (Artie tries to fire him), and the union protection inverts the power dynamic completely. 'Union this!' — presumably a middle-finger gesture — is a visual/physical comedy punchline that pays off the entire brotherhood arc. Among the episode's highest-impact moments.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: He's got this friend nicolae. Whew. What a mouth on that one.

jokes.text: And, Joel, are you an ape or a monkey? / Should I throw it? Is she gonna take the ball? / Ha! Now you know how I feel, pal.
jokes.setup: Following the argument with Nicolae, Artie finds someone apparently handling an animal (presumably a chimp, per the earlier mention).
jokes.punchline: 'Now you know how I feel' — Artie identifies with the animal trainer's uncertainty about an unpredictable creature, connecting it to his own experience managing Larry Sanders.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the chimp/balls story is elegant — we now see a chimp handler on set, and Artie's 'Now you know how I feel' links the animal's unpredictability directly to Larry. It's thematically tight, it pays off the earlier philosophical speech, and it's funny on its own terms (identifying with a chimp trainer). Also: 'Are you an ape or a monkey?' as a serious question is a small delight.

jokes.text: And he's smiling like that because his refund check from the Betty Ford Clinic just came in the mail today.
jokes.setup: Larry has just praised Artie on air; Artie is taking a bow and smiling.
jokes.punchline: Larry explains Artie's smile as being caused by a Betty Ford Clinic refund check — casually outing Artie's substance abuse history to the live audience.
jokes.explanation: The callback to Artie's substance abuse history (established via the DUI reference) lands here with extra weight — and it's delivered live, publicly, as a joke. Larry roasting Artie while supposedly honoring him is a distillation of their dynamic. 'Refund check from Betty Ford' is a specific, witty construction. Artie's one-word response ('Prick') is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Prick.
jokes.setup: Larry has just publicly joked about Artie's Betty Ford history on air.
jokes.punchline: Artie's single-word aside — 'Prick' — to no one in particular is the most economical possible response: affectionate, true, resigned.
jokes.explanation: One word. One word that encapsulates the entire Larry-Artie relationship, the entire episode, and Artie's entire worldview. 'Prick' said to no one, about Larry, by a man who just took a public bow — it is simultaneously an insult, a term of endearment, and a professional summary. Economy is as high as it gets: 10/10. Character integration is near-perfect — only Artie says this, only in this moment, only after this episode's journey. This is the episode's best pure line.

jokes.text: It's going to be a good one tonight. I feel it.
jokes.setup: The morning after — Artie arrives fresh, optimistic.
jokes.punchline: Given everything we've just seen (the argument, the drinking, the janitor, the watch, the firing), his breezy confidence is deeply ironic and slightly absurd.
jokes.explanation: The morning reset is a structural joke — Artie's resilience is both admirable and slightly insane given last night. Works as a closing ironic button.

jokes.text: Artie, the karaoke machine. / Trouble, Hank? / No, that's just the point. Everything is Dan-Dan-dandy.
jokes.setup: Hank brings up the karaoke machine that was previously causing a crisis.
jokes.punchline: The crisis has resolved itself — everything is 'Dan-Dan-dandy' — and Artie's calm is juxtaposed with Hank's earlier outrage.
jokes.explanation: The karaoke machine running gag gets its resolution — 'Dan-Dan-dandy' is Hank's characterful vocabulary. The joke is partly that the entire earlier crisis has quietly resolved and Hank is now breezy about it.

jokes.text: It appears that someone has vomited in my wastebasket... / I'll get on it right away. / I said to myself, 'well, did I do that?' / But I don't think I did. / Who'd we have on the show last night?
jokes.setup: Hank reports mysterious vomit in his wastebasket and wonders if he did it himself.
jokes.punchline: The comedy is in Hank genuinely not knowing if he vomited in his own wastebasket — combined with his asking who was on the show last night as if to narrow down suspects.
jokes.explanation: Hank's puzzlement about whether he's responsible for the vomit in his own waste bin is beautifully in character — his self-absorption means he genuinely treats this as a mystery. 'Did I do that?' / 'I don't think I did' is a perfect small comedy beat. 'Who'd we have on the show last night?' as a detective pivot is absurdly logical.

jokes.text: I believe random vomit is the janitor's responsibility. / Have Brian call and ask for Nicolae. / Is he in? / Yes.
jokes.setup: Hank asks how to handle the mysterious wastebasket vomit.
jokes.punchline: Artie sends for Nicolae — the Romanian janitor he befriended (and then argued with and fired) last night. 'Is he in? Yes.' confirms Nicolae is still employed, despite being 'fired.'
jokes.explanation: The callback is efficient and funny: Artie sending for the man he 'fired' last night (who is still there because of union protection) is the perfect morning-after resolution. 'Is he in? Yes.' confirms the universe righted itself. Great structural payoff.

jokes.text: I'm going to say a few words that'll really make you smile. / OK. / Warm, moist, muffin-y goodness. / Courtney Cox? / Oh, close. A muffin.
jokes.setup: Artie teases Larry with a promise of something smile-inducing, then says 'warm, moist, muffin-y goodness.'
jokes.punchline: Larry hears the description and thinks 'Courtney Cox' — making the implicit explicit in a way that's both flattering to Cox and revealing about Larry's mind. 'Oh, close. A muffin' is the deflating return to reality.
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent: 'warm, moist, muffin-y goodness' is loaded enough to prompt Larry's response, but innocent enough that Artie can plausibly have meant a muffin the whole time. Larry's 'Courtney Cox?' reveals his inner monologue. 'Oh, close. A muffin. All right. Well, even better.' is a perfect layered button — Artie pretending a muffin is close to Courtney Cox while also suggesting it might be better. One of the episode's tightest constructed jokes.

jokes.text: Is he in? / Yes. / Have you, by chance, gone through his voice-mail messages? / Yes. And he only got one. From Jack Levitz in publicity. / That's the only one he got? / No, but that's the only one he heard.
jokes.setup: Artie checks whether Larry heard the voicemail he left the previous night.
jokes.punchline: Larry got multiple messages — but only listened to one (from publicity). The 3:15 AM voicemail of 'scum-sucking asshole / limp-dicked pantywaist / hope your balls fall off' is unheard.
jokes.explanation: The structure of 'that's the only one he got / no, but that's the only one he heard' is beautifully crafted — the distinction between 'received' and 'heard' is the entire joke. Larry's negligence (not listening to voicemails) has accidentally protected him from Artie's fury. The comedy of Artie's relief is implied. Strong callback payoff.

jokes.text: Listen, I told Beverly to place a call to Ryan O'Neal, and I'm going to tell him that it was my fault he was bumped, OK? / Not really necessary, my boy. The storm is past.
jokes.setup: Larry wants to make amends with Ryan O'Neal for being bumped, taking responsibility.
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately deflates Larry's gesture with 'Not really necessary, the storm is past' — having already handled the relationship without Larry's input.
jokes.explanation: Artie's quiet competence — having already managed the Ryan situation — undercuts Larry's moment of good intention. The joke is that Artie cleaned it up overnight, as he always does.

jokes.text: Oh, you forgot his muffin fork.
jokes.setup: Artie is being handed something — presumably the Glenlivet Larry bought him.
jokes.punchline: The addition of 'his muffin fork' implies Artie has specific silverware requirements for muffin consumption — an absurdly specific detail that elevates his character to something slightly regal.
jokes.explanation: The muffin fork is the perfect button on the muffin bit. 'His muffin fork' — possessive, specific — implies Artie carries or has been given a dedicated fork for muffins. The absurdity is in the specificity. Maximum economy: three words.

jokes.text: Oh, you forgot his muffin fork.
jokes.setup: Larry brings Artie a muffin as a peace offering.
jokes.punchline: Artie notes that Larry forgot to bring a muffin fork — implying that muffins require specific cutlery, or that Artie has a personal muffin protocol.
jokes.explanation: Three words ('muffin fork') that are both absurd and absolutely believable for Artie. The comedy is the specificity — not just a fork, a muffin fork — which implies a world of elaborate food ritual. It's also a perfect button on the muffin joke and characterizes Artie's standards. High economy, high character integration.

jokes.text: Beverly, cancel the call to Ryan O'Neal, please. / Hmm? / Uh, sorry. Just cancel it.
jokes.setup: Larry had asked Beverly to call Ryan O'Neal so he could apologize personally.
jokes.punchline: The moment Artie signals it's already handled, Larry instantly drops his good-faith gesture — canceling the call before it's even made. Larry's moral effort has a very short half-life.
jokes.explanation: Larry's instant abandonment of his gesture of accountability — the moment it's no longer necessary — is a sharp, character-specific laugh. 'Uh, sorry. Just cancel it' is the deflated self-awareness of a man who was never really going to do it anyway.

jokes.text: You told him that I didn't hear the message, right? / Yeah. / Good, good. / How bad was it? / Bad. Not as bad as the one he left me last year. / He's got this friend Nicolae. Whew. What a mouth on that one.
jokes.setup: Larry checks whether Beverly protected him from Artie's voicemail.
jokes.punchline: Beverly says the message was bad — but references Nicolae as having an even worse mouth. Nicolae, the Romanian janitor, has become a byword for extreme profanity after one night.
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke is one of its best. The callback to the voicemail with the added reveal that Nicolae — who enthusiastically contributed 'hope your balls fall off' — is considered to have the worse mouth is a perfect payoff. It retroactively elevates Nicolae's role and perfectly closes the episode's comedic arc. Larry's 'Beverly!' as the button — presumably recognizing he almost heard it — is the final beat.

jokes.text: Beverly!
jokes.setup: Beverly has just revealed the existence of the voicemail and Nicolae's role.
jokes.punchline: Larry's sudden fearful/outraged call of 'Beverly!' is the button — his panic at nearly knowing what was said, or his delayed horror at what he's learning.
jokes.explanation: The episode's final word — just 'Beverly!' as a reaction — is a perfect closing beat. Maximum economy (one word), strong character integration (Larry's panic is unmistakable), and it closes the episode on Larry's characteristic anxiety rather than resolution.

tmdb_overview: After a particularly trying day at work, Arthur spends the night at the studio with two new friends, Nicolae the janitor and Hank's karoake machine, and one old bottle of booze.
